title: Fix YAML scalar comment boundaries and continuation indentation
description:
Fix the post-merge review findings from #33: converting YAML strings to block style could absorb following comments into their values, and removing parent indentation could panic on quoted continuations.

Ordinary scalars remain plain or quoted when a following comment would enter a new block body. Flow expansion carries the enclosing collection's comment boundary to its final scalar, including nested collections whose closing delimiters disappear. Explicit Markdown targets still format, using deeper content indentation when needed to keep comments outside the value.

Quoted continuation lines retain their indentation when the parent moves left. This handles continuations left of the opening quote and keeps quoted `---` and `...` content away from the document-marker column. Moving a parent right still shifts its continuation lines.

Internally, the comment check reuses the source line index. Ordinary scalar checks run only after block-layout eligibility; flow expansion checks the enclosing boundary once. The changes add no decoding pass or comment-check allocation.

Four CLI transcripts and 330 external regression cases cover independent YAML 1.2 values, comments and directives, nested flow expansion, explicit Markdown targets, escapes and properties, LF/CRLF/CR, and second-pass byte idempotence. The regressions were confirmed failing before their corresponding fixes.

The complete `scripts/check.sh` gate passes locally on macOS, including Rust formatting and Clippy, public allocation checks, YAML Test Suite conformance, 1,846 external tests, and 61 editor tests. The updated reference page was rendered with Quarto. Windows and Linux were not run locally.

Paired release-build comparisons show no substantial performance regression on this Mac:

| Workload                                  | Merged #33 CPU | Fixed CPU | Change |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------: | --------: | -----: |
| Representative corpus: 400 files, 8.59 MB |       1.0332 s |  1.0422 s | +0.87% |
| Ordinary configuration, 2.36 MB           |       66.51 ms |  66.53 ms | +0.03% |
| Multiline quoted prose, 4.83 MB           |       64.53 ms |  65.44 ms | +1.40% |
| 32,000 quoted-to-literal conversions      |       30.77 ms |  32.11 ms | +4.38% |
| 32,000 flow/comment controls              |       49.25 ms |  50.44 ms | +2.41% |

Across 13 equivalent-output large controls, CPU changes range from -0.18% to +4.38%. Peak RSS is essentially unchanged; the largest increase is 0.16 MiB on a roughly 38 MiB Markdown workload. Representative elapsed medians are 5.2285 to 5.3479 seconds (+2.28%), with overlapping samples. All 400 representative outputs match across binaries. All 16 large cases verify and remain byte-idempotent on the fixed binary; three unsafe-comment cases intentionally change output and are excluded from the equivalent-work comparison.

Measured frozen, locked release builds of `d9af714` and `a220046` (this PR's implementation) on an Apple M4 Max, macOS 26.7.2 ARM64, Rust 1.99.1. Large cases use 11 repetitions after two warmups per binary; the representative corpus uses five after one warmup, with a separate CLI process per file. Binary order alternates. Timings include CLI launch, formatting, and writes; input restoration and output hashing are outside the timer.

title: Reflow multiline YAML prose while preserving scalar values
description:
Format long prose already split across plain, single-quoted, or double-quoted YAML continuation lines. Supported multiline quoted values allow surrounding collections to format while preserving comments and decoded whitespace.

Preserved values retain their parent keys or sequence markers, including shared headers in compact nested sequences. Parent tags, anchors, comments, and intervening trivia survive ordinary, Markdown, and embedded scalar formatting. Containers keep indentation compatible with retained entries while editable siblings still format. Converted literal bodies follow the emitted header's indentation, and root block scalars retain leading comments and document markers.

Keep scalar boundaries consistent across parsing, layout, and verification:

- Recognize dash-prefixed mapping keys such as `-1` and `-lorem` separately from sequence markers.
- Normalize multiline quoted values before compacting collections, with width planning based on the emitted spelling.
- Distinguish tabs after required block indentation, including tab-only content lines, from unsupported tab indentation.
- Interpret explicit block indentation indicators relative to the enclosing container, preserving meaningful Markdown code indentation when headers move.
- Keep dedented block-scalar comments outside values during parsing and emission, so file-scoped and next-node directives remain active.

Internally, formatting and verification share multiline scalar decoding, and parent properties participate in semantic verification without becoming scalar content. Markdown block scalars are parsed when their target becomes known, including parent-line tags. Their owned source removes YAML indentation before Markdown parsing and retains original diagnostic coordinates. Skip and template preservation boundaries remain intact.

Internal performance changes reuse decoded scalar text and borrowed wrapped lines, defer ordinary Markdown wrapping plans until directive policy settles, and recycle line buffers. Markdown block-start checks use the parser's list-marker grammar, avoiding repeated full-line scans for ordinary words ending in a period. Explicit-target diagnostics, skip behavior, and verification remain covered by public tests.

Blank embedded output is rejected when it would absorb a following indented YAML comment. The file remains unchanged; rewriting the comment's indentation or the embedded target's scalar style is unsupported.

Public CLI transcripts and external tests cover independent YAML 1.2 value comparisons, comments and properties, compact ancestors, directives, indentation, line endings, and second-pass byte idempotence. Standalone Markdown semantic tests invoke Quarto's bundled Pandoc directly; a regression checks formatting and semantic equality with the Quarto runtime unavailable.

Validation: new public allocation regressions fail on the earlier PR build and pass with these changes. New public CLI regressions were confirmed failing before their fixes. The complete `scripts/check.sh` gate passes locally on macOS, including Rust formatting and Clippy, CLI transcripts, YAML Test Suite conformance, 1,516 external tests, and 61 editor tests.

The default benchmark now uses a deterministic eight-family corpus covering ordinary configs, flow and block collections, multiline plain and quoted prose, Unicode and escapes, CRLF literal scalars, one/two/eight-paragraph Markdown, and rich Markdown. It keeps the existing 400-file and repetition budgets; individual families remain selectable. Corpus metadata, artifact names, and R summary filters keep these results separate from historical flow-heavy measurements. The large-file and published directory comparisons retain their existing corpora.

Public benchmark regressions cover deterministic generation, family coverage, verification, idempotence, and historical result separation. All 400 default inputs also passed a separate verification and second-pass byte comparison. With a frozen release binary, the broader default completed in 22.8–24.5 seconds locally, including generation, one warmup, and two measured repetitions; the old flow-heavy corpus took 23.6–24.0 seconds in the same alternating comparison. These timings exclude compilation.

Performance measured on an Apple M4 Max, macOS 26.7.1, using Rust 1.99.1 locked release builds: main `07ca683` versus PR `049dd4c`. General YAML controls retain about 3–5% CPU overhead and essentially unchanged memory. Equivalent-work Markdown and prose fixtures are faster than main.

Paired end-to-end CLI medians, with identical output on main and this PR:

| Workload                                |     Main |       PR | CPU change vs main | Peak RSS, main → PR |
| --------------------------------------- | -------: | -------: | -----------------: | ------------------: |
| 4.00 MB YAML                            | 118.5 ms | 123.0 ms |              +4.7% |     50.7 → 50.7 MiB |
| 4.01 MB Markdown                        | 117.5 ms | 102.0 ms |              -6.1% |     18.3 → 18.1 MiB |
| 4.00 MB Markdown with YAML front matter | 115.8 ms | 120.9 ms |              -5.9% |     20.0 → 19.7 MiB |
| 32,000 Markdown scalars                 | 249.3 ms | 204.4 ms |             -21.8% |     95.3 → 80.9 MiB |
| 32,000 single-line quoted prose values  | 176.1 ms | 147.6 ms |             -27.8% |     61.0 → 60.8 MiB |

Separate block-heavy and flow-heavy YAML controls use 2.8% and 3.4% more CPU than main, with identical output and essentially unchanged memory. Elapsed-time samples on the general controls overlap substantially; small wall-time differences should not be treated as precise formatter costs.

Synthetic workloads with 32,000 scalar entries exercise newly supported behavior. Default formatting, without `--verify`:

| Workload                       |   Input |     Main |       PR | Peak RSS, main → PR |
| ------------------------------ | ------: | -------: | -------: | ------------------: |
| Multiline plain prose          | 7.36 MB | 129.5 ms | 152.6 ms |     62.0 → 63.5 MiB |
| Multiline double-quoted prose  | 7.42 MB | 149.5 ms | 170.1 ms |     62.2 → 62.3 MiB |
| Inline-tagged Markdown scalars | 6.02 MB | 173.4 ms | 232.1 ms |   128.9 → 140.0 MiB |
| Parent-tagged Markdown scalars | 6.27 MB | 112.3 ms | 232.0 ms |    60.2 → 145.5 MiB |

These rows include additional work. Multiline prose is now decoded and wrapped. Markdown is parsed after removing YAML indentation: main treats the inline-tagged fixture as indented code, and drops the tag from the parent-tagged fixture, skipping its Markdown preparation. Those lower baseline costs do not represent equivalent formatting. The PR retains a dedented source and parsed document for each Markdown scalar.

With `--verify`, the plain, double-quoted, inline Markdown, and parent-tagged Markdown cases take 226.3, 226.3, 311.6, and 321.8 ms. Their main baselines are 199.6, 193.7, 271.5, and 195.8 ms respectively. Markdown peak RSS is 155.5 MiB inline and 171.4 MiB parent-tagged.

Compared with the earlier PR build `f4713f6`, the optimizations reduce these scalar workloads' elapsed time by 12–25% and CPU time by 19–34%, including verification cases, with identical output. Markdown peak RSS falls by about 21 MiB without verification and 16–17 MiB with verification. Public allocation regressions cover multiline prose, nested Markdown parsing and formatting, and line-buffer reuse.

Method: 15 measured repetitions after two warmups per binary and workload. Runs rotate through all six orders of main, the earlier PR build, and the optimized build. Timings include CLI launch, formatting, and file writes; input restoration and output checks are outside the timer. Generated inputs are identical. All 15 workloads have deterministic output identical to the earlier PR build, and a separate pass confirms second-pass byte idempotence. The five general controls and two equivalent-work controls also match main. CPU time and peak RSS use per-process accounting. Measurements are local to this Mac.

A separate check on 23 held-out workloads compares the optimization commit `049dd4c` with `f4713f6`, using 11 repetitions after two warmups. It varies scalar length, escaping, Unicode, CRLF and blank lines, indentation, prose and Markdown wrap widths, Markdown paragraph counts, real list markers, rich Markdown, and preservation-heavy input. Wrapped plain prose uses 14–16% less CPU; Unicode and escaped quotes use 31–37% less. Markdown without sentence periods uses about 4–8% less CPU, including documents with multiple paragraphs. Rich Markdown changes by about 1% without verification and 9% with verification; genuine list-marker cases show little change.

A batch of 96 public YAML files from uv, CPython, ragnar, and pkgdown is essentially unchanged: 28.4→28.3 ms CPU, with 77 files formatted and 19 left unchanged. It uses explicit file paths, so it excludes directory discovery and per-file process startup. All 23 held-out workloads produce identical output before and after the optimization and pass second-pass byte idempotence. This broader evidence supports improvements to eligible scalar and nested Markdown paths; it does not establish a universal YAML speedup. The public sample mainly covers CI and documentation configuration, and all measurements are from one Mac.

title: Refactor formatter modules and fix CLI and editor bugs
description:
Separate formatter, workspace, and acceptance-test responsibilities to make the large implementation files easier to maintain, and fix six behavior bugs found during the review. Mechanical extractions retain the existing public Rust entry points and one Cargo package.

## User-facing fixes

- Relative file, directory, and stdin paths discover `yamark.toml` above the working directory.
- Unified diffs merge overlapping context so nearby changes produce applicable patches.
- Git filter adoption, joining, and checking handle filenames that Git would quote in line-oriented output, including non-UTF-8 names on Unix.
- Git filter verification with `--repo` reads configuration from the selected repository, including nested configuration files.
- YAML flow layout counts required quotes around escaped numeric-looking strings, keeping formatting stable on a second pass.
- Editor formatting discards results when the document changes and retains the selection range captured when formatting starts.

## Internal changes

- Split YAML parsing, planning, scalar handling, and emission; Markdown block parsing and wrapping; Git filter operations; and workspace traversal and diff rendering into focused private modules.
- Split the large CLI and editor acceptance-test files by contract, preserving existing assertions and adding public regressions for the fixes.
- Document development practices, implementation ownership, and test organization; move historical workpads and experiments into `design-sketches/`.
- Execute the feature-specific diagnostic tests in the shared check script and correct a fixture whose string literal accidentally removed indentation.
- Run the Git path regression tests on Linux to cover non-UTF-8 filenames in the working tree.

title: Fix formatter regressions and Windows build/test support
description:
Fixes #25. Ruff's notebook output can remove the final LF from a CRLF pair, leaving closing fences or YAML scalar boundaries malformed. Complete that pair in the shared external-formatter output helper, and repair the formatter regressions and Windows failures uncovered while validating it.

User-facing changes:
- Keep sentence wrapping active around inline HTML in Markdown lists and blockquotes while preserving raw HTML block boundaries.
- Keep `git-filter adopt` and `join` compatible with `core.autocrlf` and explicit `eol` attributes by applying Git's checkout conversion and refreshing its cached file metadata.
- Run benchmarks on Windows with `.exe` paths, platform temporary directories, and npm `.cmd`/`.bat` launchers. Preserve literal filenames containing shell characters and propagate formatter exit codes.
- Report Windows benchmark CPU and peak RSS as unavailable, with null samples and an explanatory status, because launcher-only counters omit child processes. Elapsed time, throughput, and output validation remain available.

Internal changes:
- Add byte-exact newline regressions and Git integration transcripts. Adoption cases check exact staged and checkout bytes for CRLF, LF, and explicit `eol` overrides.
- Keep source/transcript checkouts at LF while preserving byte-sensitive fixtures; replace portable test stubs' Unix shell dependencies with Python and correct Windows path expectations.
- Isolate pytest temporary directories and wheel-install tool directories. Restrict Unix shell fixtures to Unix and skip symlink creation only when Windows lacks the required privilege.
- Run CI on both macOS and Windows and document local prerequisites.

The existing 18 CPU-scaling checks still require Unix `wait4`; Unix packaging and fake-shell-executable checks remain covered by the macOS job.

title: Preserve link destinations and container block boundaries
description:
Column and sentence-and-column wrapping keep empty link destinations as `()` and keep angle-bracket destinations on the same line as the label. This prevents a blank line from breaking empty links and prevents Pandoc Markdown from treating `<` and `>` as URL characters. The fix also applies to images and linked images. Ordinary nonempty destinations retain their existing wrapping layout.

For example, both of these remain intact with `--wrap 12`, even when they exceed the requested width:

```markdown
[empty destination]()

[text](<https://example.com>)
```

Container wrapping preserves authored headings and the boundaries of HTML blocks. A `<pre>` block in a list or blockquote stays on its own line, with its contents unchanged. Text resembling headings inside multiline code no longer suppresses sentence wrapping around that code.

Internally, container preparation uses the existing inline scanner before deciding whether to preserve source lines. CLI transcripts and public API checks cover lists, blockquotes, linked images, line endings, and repeat formatting. Link rendering and sentence/column roundtrip tests use Pandoc's Markdown reader and Multimark's cmark-gfm parser for CommonMark and GFM; container rendering tests cover Pandoc's Markdown, CommonMark, and GFM readers.

Validation: `scripts/check.sh` passed in full, including formatting, Clippy, the Rust test suites, all 224 CLI transcripts, 397 external tests, and 57 editor tests. The new link and container regression cases were confirmed failing before their fixes. Ruff checks on the changed Python tests also passed.

title: Preserve Markdown structure when wrapping sentences
description: Sentence wrapping can move punctuation such as `-`, `2.`, `>`, or `#` to the start of a line, changing prose into a list, blockquote, or heading. These punctuation sequences are Markdown markers; literal markers are those intended as ordinary text. Escape supported literal markers at new sentence boundaries so `--wrap sentence` and `--wrap sentence:` preserve their meaning. Keep meaning-sensitive boundaries joined while continuing to wrap at safe boundaries. The scope is safe marker escaping and column roundtrips in prose recognized by the existing formatter. Preserve meaning and idempotence when that conflicts with sentence or column boundaries. Ambiguous boundaries stay joined; paragraphs containing raw TeX environments remain unchanged. Sentence and column wrapping also preserve paragraphs containing unescaped raw HTML openers (`x. Opening sentence. (b) value. ``` becomes: ```text HTML x. Opening sentence. (b\) value. ``` Preserve the contents of `$$…$$` and `\(…\)` math, including escaped closing delimiters. Inside emphasis, stars in matched math do not close the surrounding emphasis: `Text *use \(x^* + 2\) here*.` keeps both math delimiters with `--wrap 72`. Keep asterisk escapes when another asterisk could form emphasis under a supported reader, including readers with math syntax disabled. With `--wrap 12`, `Literal \* \(x * y\)` becomes: ```text Literal \* \(x * y\) ``` Escaped punctuation such as `\*.` cannot form emphasis, so `Literal \*. Opening sentence. * value.` becomes: ```text Literal \*. Opening sentence. \* value. ``` A standalone `\*` remains conservative when another asterisk is present: column wrapping may remove its escape, so keeping that boundary joined preserves the column roundtrip. Necessary asterisk escapes also survive a compact backslash hard break before emphasized text on the next line. Spaced asterisks also remain conservative: `Math 2 * 3. Opening sentence. * value.` keeps the last two sentences joined. Pandoc can interpret the arithmetic star as an emphasis opener if column reflow puts a newline after it. Keep delimiter-sensitive repairs joined: `Before. *** *word*` stays on one line with `--wrap sentence:72`, and `something * *** |` stays on one line at width 12. A trailing literal asterisk stays with the following emphasized text during ordinary wrapping and backtracking. At width 23, `Costs* *include taxes* (b) details.` becomes: ```text Costs* *include taxes* (b\) details. ``` When a possible emphasis closer depends on backslash math support, keep it with the following prose. With `--wrap 24`, `Text *use \(x^* + 2\) here* and *more*.` becomes: ```text Text *use \(x^* + 2\) here* and *more*. ``` Asterisks inside HTML attributes or simple matched emphasis do not suppress safe sentence breaks. An earlier unpaired asterisk or asterisks inside the emphasis retain the conservative guard, because reflow can change how supported readers pair those delimiters. Shortcode arguments are excluded from the math-opener scan. The shortcode regression is checked with repeated formatting and `--check`. For example, `Em *x*. Opening sentence. * value.` becomes: ```text Em *x*. Opening sentence. \* value. ``` For example, both `Before after.` and `The operator ` in an HTML tag are also preserved: `Before after.` retains its literal attribute backslash. Recognized code and math spans retain their internal whitespace even when the paragraph is left unwrapped; ordinary trailing whitespace outside those spans still cleans up. Definition-list boundaries stay joined: `Term sentence. ~ definition-looking prose. Last sentence.` becomes: ```text Term sentence. ~ definition-looking prose. Last sentence. ``` `~word` and `~~struck text~~` remain ordinary inline content and can start a wrapped sentence. Unsafe inline HTML and setext-heading boundaries also stay joined. With `--wrap sentence`, `Opening. - word. --` becomes: ```text Opening. \- word. -- ``` Reference-definition checks require a colon immediately after the matching label bracket. For example, `Opening. [x] text ]: still prose.` becomes: ```text Opening. [x] text ]: still prose. ``` Parsing and wrap safety share this boundary, preserving real definitions, escaped brackets, and column roundtrips. Headings inside quotes and lists retain their authored lines and escapes. For example, both `> # Title \#` and this underlined heading stay unchanged during sentence and column wrapping: ```text > Title > ----- ``` Ordinary quote and list prose continues to wrap at safe boundaries. Internally, sentence and column layout share marker repair and account for added and removed escapes. Layout reads retained token ranges, recognizes ordinary prose before constructing candidate lines, and checks sentence endings after applying escapes. Combined wrapping reuses the marker repair performed after each token instead of repeating it before the next token. A shared scan checks math and asterisk hazards using existing inline boundaries. Math scanning preserves complete spans and indexes unescaped closing delimiters once. CLI transcripts and public API checks cover containers, hard breaks, formatting skips, line endings, idempotence, column → sentence → column roundtrips, and allocation growth for long plain sentences. Rendering checks use Pandoc's Markdown, CommonMark, GFM, and `markdown+tex_math_single_backslash` readers. The test setup uses the current Quarto release in CI and accepts the locally installed version. Matching release builds on Apple silicon gave these median CPU times for approximately 4 MB generated documents. The baseline is main (`ff3160b5`), built from a clean source archive with the same toolchain and lockfile; the measured PR source matches `6cc3756`. Each row uses 24 measured runs per revision after warmup, with run order balanced and reversed. These are local CPU measurements; elapsed timings were more variable. | Document | Wrap | Main | This PR | Median paired change | | ------------------------------------------ | ------------- | -------: | -------: | -------------------: | | Mixed Markdown | `default` | 70.4 ms | 66.5 ms | -4.7% | | Mixed Markdown | `sentence:72` | 62.7 ms | 63.3 ms | +1.1% | | Prose containing Markdown-like punctuation | `sentence:72` | 117.9 ms | 135.5 ms | +17.9% | | One long paragraph | `sentence:72` | 40.5 ms | 43.0 ms | +6.3% | Paired changes are the median of per-run percentages. Default Markdown and the long paragraph produce identical output on both revisions. Mixed Markdown with sentence wrapping and the document containing these punctuation examples produce different output because of the correctness fixes. Peak memory is similar for default Markdown and the long paragraph. Peak memory for the punctuation examples rises from about 82 MiB to 95 MiB. Fixes #27.

title: Preserve outer list paragraphs after nested lists
description:
Keep paragraphs after a nested Markdown list inside their outer list item. Wrapping previously removed the paragraph's indentation and split the list. These layouts now remain intact through the existing list preservation behavior, including when blank lines precede or separate nested items.

Ambiguous sibling, empty-item, child-heading, and mixed list/raw layouts retain their original indentation for GFM and Pandoc compatibility. This keeps fenced and raw block contents intact while allowing prose outside the preserved region to be formatted. Heading-like content inside child fences and inline literals continues to use the existing formatting behavior.

Internally, the list scanner retains the outer item's content boundary through nested items and tracks the lowest list indentation for lazy prose. Marker boundaries stay separate from task-checkbox alignment. Mixed list/raw regions are consumed together, with an incremental inline scan that skips confirmed raw blocks, avoiding repeated scans of the remaining document.

CLI transcripts cover the reported example and compatibility boundaries. Additional CLI checks cover wrap modes, line endings, second passes, and scaling with alternating lists and fences.

Fixes #26.

Treat double-brace templates as opaque words
description:
Treat `{{` through the first literal `}}` as one opaque word in supported Markdown prose, so surrounding text can wrap without interpreting a template language. Quotes and nested braces do not affect that boundary, and contents can span lines.

Add the exact default delimiter pair `{{< raw >}}` / `{{< /raw >}}` to preserve its whole payload. The longest opening string wins; the first literal closing string ends the span, with no nested-tag matching. Tags with arguments or different spacing keep the ordinary `{{` / `}}` behavior. Custom pairs can opt into literal matching:

```toml
[template]
add_delimiters = [
  { open = "[[raw]]", close = "[[/raw]]", literal = true }
]
```

These examples compare output from main (`d2e04dd`) and this PR for identical inputs with `--wrap paragraph --canonical`.

**The raw pair preserves spaces, emphasis, and link spelling in its payload.**

Before (`main`):

```text
Before
{{< raw >}}
Keep *this* [link](target).
{{< /raw >}}
after *word*.
```

After (this PR):

```text
Before {{< raw >}}
Keep   _this_ [link](  target  ).
{{< /raw >}} after *word*.
```

**Other shortcode-looking words wrap with surrounding prose.**

Before (`main`):

```text
Before
{{< meta title >}}
after *word*.
```

After (this PR):

```text
Before {{< meta title >}} after *word*.
```

**The first literal closer ends a double-brace word, even inside quoted-looking text.**

Before (`main`):

```text
Before {{ render("}}", "keep   this _raw_") }} after *word*.
```

After (this PR):

```text
Before {{ render("}}", "keep this *raw*") }} after *word*.
```

**Line breaks inside a word stay intact while surrounding prose joins it.**

Before (`main`):

```text
Before
{{< meta
 title >}}
after *word*.
```

After (this PR):

```text
Before {{< meta
 title >}} after *word*.
```

An unfinished double-brace word or literal pair preserves the remainder of its Markdown fragment. Standalone words use normal final-newline insertion, and `fmt: skip` targets the whole Markdown paragraph. Use `fmt: skip` or `fmt: off` / `fmt: on` to preserve layout. Other delimiter pairs keep their existing single-line quote and brace handling unless configured with `literal = true`. Headings, tables, and embedded source strings/comments apply the generic template policy to shortcode-looking text too.

Internally, remove the shortcode scanner, node, and emission path. Reuse inline literal spans and keep multiline words together during paragraph collection. Literal pairs use direct closing-string searches; the raw strings are default configuration data rather than scanner rules. Borrow default delimiter strings so copying configurations does not allocate each marker.

Rust API: remove `MarkdownNodeKind::Shortcode` and `contains_markdown_template_span`; use `contains_template_span` for template detection. `TemplateDelimiter` gains a `literal` field; its `open` and `close` fields use `Cow<'static, str>` to borrow default strings.

## Performance

Compared the complete PR (`58a60b0`) with main (`d2e04dd`) using matching Rust 1.98.1 release builds on an Apple M4 Max/macOS. Each workload ran in two batches of 11 alternating main/PR pairs, with warmups and reversed order in the second batch. The table uses approximately 4 MB inputs; template-heavy cases repeat the same paragraph thousands of times. CPU times are medians of child user plus system time; percentage changes are medians of paired changes.

| Input                                           | Main CPU (ms) | PR CPU (ms) | CPU change | Identical output |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------: | ----------: | ---------: | ---------------- |
| Ordinary Markdown                               |          74.9 |        74.7 |      -0.3% | Yes              |
| Prose with short physical lines                 |          73.5 |        77.5 |      +5.2% | Yes              |
| One shortcode paragraph per 20 plain paragraphs |          75.4 |        83.5 |      +9.9% | Yes              |
| Dense inline `{{< meta title >}}` words         |         152.3 |       223.9 |     +52.0% | Yes              |
| Shortcodes on separate source lines             |         108.7 |       240.2 |    +119.4% | No               |
| Multiline `{{< meta` / `title >}}` words        |          44.3 |       257.0 |    +489.1% | No               |
| Multiline words with block-looking contents     |         121.0 |       179.6 |     +48.4% | No               |
| Whole-line raw pairs                            |          17.7 |        61.3 |    +245.7% | Yes              |
| Ordinary `{{ expression }}` words               |         238.5 |       216.3 |      -8.9% | Yes              |
| Long `{{ expression }}` words                   |          50.2 |        17.2 |     -65.6% | Yes              |
| Raw bodies on separate lines                    |          83.2 |        54.2 |     -35.2% | No               |
| Raw bodies between surrounding prose            |         170.9 |        77.7 |     -54.6% | No               |

There are substantial regressions on some dense template inputs. Inline Quarto-style words take 52% more CPU with identical output. Whole-line raw pairs take about 3.5 times as much CPU with identical output (18 to 61 ms); main copies those lines through its standalone shortcode path, while the PR uses the generic paragraph/literal pipeline. Multiline Quarto words take about 5.9 times as much CPU (44 to 257 ms), with changed output: the PR formats surrounding prose that main leaves untouched. These regressions appeared in all 22 measured pairs. Simpler closing-delimiter recognition saves work inside expressions, but paragraph boundary scans and generic protected-span handling add work elsewhere.

Generic expressions are faster with unchanged output: about 9% for ordinary expressions and 66% for long expressions. Raw-body cases on separate lines or between prose are 35–55% faster, but their output and work change because payloads are now preserved instead of formatted. Repeated unfinished openers also get faster; increasing the count from 32,000 to 128,000 raises PR CPU from 2.9 to 4.7 ms, with no superlinear growth observed over that range.

For smaller inputs, the approximately 40 KB dense inline/standalone/multiline Quarto cases add about 1.0/1.5/2.4 ms of CPU; paired median elapsed increases are about 1.6/1.9/3.0 ms. Ordinary 40 KB Markdown changes by less than 0.1 ms of CPU. A directory of 19 actual Markdown/Quarto documents from main (141 KB total) takes 17.4 versus 17.6 ms elapsed and 13.1 versus 12.6 ms CPU, so that corpus shows no noticeable slowdown. Eighteen outputs match; one template-documentation paragraph changes wrapping. YAML stays near unchanged; the 4 MB front-matter case adds about 2 ms of CPU (+2.6%). These are workload-specific results from one machine; elapsed time includes process launch and is noisier than child CPU.

Peak process RSS also depends on the input. Whole-line raw pairs rise from 21.9 to 43.1 MiB; multiline Quarto words rise from 38.9 to 54.9 MiB; dense inline Quarto words rise from 36.3 to 39.7 MiB. Other cases improve: standalone shortcode lines drop from 79.0 to 51.5 MiB, generic multiline words from 79.5 to 45.2 MiB, and raw bodies on separate lines from 56.0 to 44.3 MiB. Ordinary Markdown and the real-document directory remain approximately unchanged. RSS is the process high-water mark, not live heap or allocation volume.

title: Avoid unchanged inline normalization buffers
description:
## Summary

#23 reuses unchanged inline source in retained plans, but `normalize_whole()` still builds a temporary `String` before that decision. This change keeps a borrowed source prefix during the existing normalization pass and allocates output storage on the first differing append.

## User-facing behavior

Formatting output, diagnostics, and exit status are unchanged across the measured Markdown and YAML controls.

## Internal changes

`NormalizedInline` returns borrowed or owned text. The plan consumer retains #23's source-handle reuse. Canonicalization and segmented hard-break assembly keep their owned paths; recognition, validation, token and literal offsets, emission, child fragments, and YAML are unchanged.

## Fuller measurements

The exact 4 MB standard Markdown and front-matter inputs avoid 5,995 and 5,665 whole-body output allocations, removing 2.33 MB and 2.22 MB of temporary copies. The retained short-link workload avoids 43,479 allocations and 3.91 MB of copies. Separate allocator probes confirm the same reductions in total allocation calls.

With two warmups and 32–48 balanced measured pairs, child CPU is effectively flat on standard Markdown (+0.1% paired median) and 0.5% lower on short links. A word-dense 4 MB control made of unchanged 20 KB paragraphs saves 200 allocations but costs 4.2% more CPU in column mode and 9.6% more in sentence mode. The body-length sweep shows similar costs at smaller paragraph sizes. With an equal-length soft-break change near the end, the candidate still allocates, copies 3.99 MB of prefixes, and costs 4.9% and 9.5% more CPU in those modes. Peak live heap and production RSS show no consistent improvement.

## Assessment

The allocation reduction is real, but the per-append checks introduce repeatable CPU regressions on word-dense prose without a corresponding peak-memory benefit. This draft is not recommended for merge as-is.

## Summary

This reduces retained memory in Markdown formatting without changing formatted output. On the standard 4 MB corpus, peak live heap fell 1.40 MB (20.06 to 18.72 MiB) and production peak RSS fell 1.52 MiB (21.90 to 20.38 MiB, 6.9%). The planner now pays for one byte-equality comparison per normalized inline body. title: Skip YAML AST scans without Markdown finalization plans
description:
## Summary

Plain YAML has no Markdown finalization work, yet `finalize_document()` scans its YAML AST once for inline Markdown scalar plans and `nested_emit_policies()` scans it again for nested Markdown block plans. Record a conservative flag as those emit plans are assigned, then omit both YAML AST traversals when the flag is false.

## Behavior

Formatting output, diagnostics, exit status, and public APIs are unchanged. The flag is set at initial and contextual plan assignments, including replanning after late directives. It only changes from false to true, so a plan later replaced by a preserve or skip plan can cause an extra scan but cannot suppress required finalization. Inline Markdown is covered even when there is no nested document. The existing path and order remain intact when either Markdown plan is present.

The CLI transcripts cover inline-only YAML, inline and block Markdown with late options and skip behavior, and Markdown front matter. Temporary probes showed both scans on a plain 13-node YAML document at the baseline and neither scan with the guard; Markdown controls still entered both scans. Nine differential controls, including a failing directive, matched the baseline byte for byte in stdout and stderr and had the same exit status.

title: Reflow prose around opaque inline templates
description:
Treat complete single-line templates as indivisible words so surrounding Markdown can reflow without changing any bytes inside the tokens. This applies to paragraphs, lists, blockquotes, definition lists, and already-supported Markdown fragments, using the existing delimiter configuration.

The examples below show input (`-`) and formatted output (`+`). With `--wrap sentence`, a template-only source line rejoins its paragraph:

```diff
-Before
-{{ render("keep   this") }}
-after.
+Before {{ render("keep   this") }} after.
```

With `--wrap 20`, the whole token moves to its own line. Like any long word, it may exceed the requested width:

```diff
-Before {{ customer.name }} after.
+Before
+{{ customer.name }}
+after.
```

With `--canonical --wrap sentence`, Markdown outside the expression formats normally; quoted delimiters, whitespace, and Markdown-looking contents inside remain literal:

```diff
-> Before
-> {{ render("}}", "_keep_ [x](  url  )") }}
-> after _word_ and [link](  url  ).
+> Before {{ render("}}", "_keep_ [x](  url  )") }} after *word* and [link](url).
```

Expressions support quoted and escaped arguments and nested braces without evaluating a template language. `{#` / `#}` comments end at the first literal `#}`; quotes, apostrophes, and braces inside have no special meaning. Existing hard breaks, blank lines, and block boundaries still apply. Use `fmt: skip`, `fmt: off/on`, or `fmt: skip file` to preserve layout.

Internally, protected source ranges survive normalization, canonicalization, wrapping, and emission. Placement restrictions are removed while retained plans, lazy inline preparation, and early rejection remain. Shared boundary matching handles overlapping delimiters and gives configured openers precedence over inline Markdown, without repeated suffix scans. Delimiter directives propagate into nested containers and refresh cached preservation decisions.

Based on `origin/main` at `73c304252240caa18d2aec7e72d244831c71ba32`. Adds 15 CLI transcripts, checks exact output and second-pass idempotence, and deliberately updates affected expectations. Regressions were confirmed before their fixes. `cargo test --test cli_cases`, focused tests, `scripts/check.sh`, and all 17 release scaling controls pass without relaxing performance bounds.

In local release benchmarks (15 measured runs, median child CPU), ordinary Markdown was within 0.2% of main and rejected inputs stayed comparable. The template workload took 29.59 ms versus 25.94 ms at `75b0e7d`: about 14% more CPU with identical output. Main took 9.28 ms but preserved those paragraphs instead of reflowing them, so that comparison includes newly enabled work.

Multiline templates and templates nested inside Markdown links or emphasis remain outside the supported reflow subset. Headings, tables, host-language admission rules, and independent shortcode blocks are unchanged. No new option or escaped-delimiter semantics are added. Documentation and release notes are updated. Related to #2.

title: Retain template and shortcode scaling regressions
description:
Retain 13 public CLI scaling regressions for template rejection and independent shortcode tokens. They cover unmatched backticks, nested bracket labels, incomplete HTML, unmatched braces, rejected template paragraphs, and repeated unpaired shortcode calls.

The checks retain exact formatted-output assertions, child CPU accounting, the existing sixfold growth ceiling, and a skip when `os.wait4` is unavailable. The unmatched-brace and emphasis inputs also cover the early-rejection path exercised by the discarded recognition prototype.

There are no user-facing formatting changes. The only change against main is `external-tests/corpus/test_scaling.py`; production code, existing transcripts, the test runner, and the existing YAML scaling guard are unchanged.

Broader template eligibility is deferred. Extending beyond the current ordinary-paragraph subset requires a separate decision about allowed expressions, Markdown and embedded contexts, and template-only placement. This draft does not implement that extension.

title: Avoid repeated substring scans in emphasis recognition
description:
Repeated unmatched emphasis openers make ordinary Markdown paragraphs rescan growing candidate contents. This reduces that work without changing formatting output or which emphasis spans are accepted.

`emphasis_span_at` now rejects whitespace-preceded closing candidates before examining their contents. A nonempty candidate ending in non-whitespace cannot be entirely whitespace, so the separate trim check is redundant. The first remaining candidate needs one newline check: finding a newline rejects the whole search because every later candidate contains it too. Each matcher call therefore scans candidate contents for newlines at most once.

The formatting change stays within emphasis recognition. A `cfg(test)` byte counter supports a deterministic regression through the public formatter API and is absent from ordinary builds. Escape handling, literal exclusion, delimiter runs, intraword underscores, and opaque ranges keep their existing rules. Paragraph template policy and its early rejection are unchanged; `InlineSource` preparation is unchanged. No cache, parser mode, input limit, fallback, or benchmark infrastructure is added.

## Performance

Equivalent `cargo build --release --locked` builds against main `095420c`, using Rust 1.98.1 on an Apple M4 Max with macOS 26.7. The public CLI invocation is `format --stdin-file-path input.md --wrap sentence`. For this input:

```python
"Before `code` " + " ".join("*x" for _ in range(n)) + " after.\n"
```

| Openers | Main CPU seconds | Branch CPU seconds |
| ------- | ---------------: | -----------------: |
| 400     |          0.03629 |            0.00352 |
| 800     |          0.26704 |            0.00699 |
| 1,600   |          2.07599 |            0.02040 |

These are medians of five alternating runs, except the 1,600-opener baseline uses the single initial bounded reproduction; larger pathological baseline runs were avoided. Plain prose without the code span gives the same result: 2.07903 to 0.02043 seconds at 1,600 openers. The template-bearing form retains its early rejection and takes 0.00397 to 0.00228 seconds. Adding a valid late closer takes 0.01738 to 0.00240 seconds at 3,200 openers.

This reduces the reported non-template inputs from cubic to quadratic work, not linear work. Branch-only measurements at 1,600 / 3,200 / 6,400 openers take 0.02086 / 0.07307 / 0.28262 CPU seconds. Repeated failed suffix searches remain.

Temporary counters in separate instrumented builds distinguish the two costs. At 256 openers, the code/plain inputs still make 512 matcher calls and 65,280 candidate visits. Bytes examined by newline checks fall from 16,711,680 to zero. With a valid late closer, two matcher calls examine 1,542 bytes instead of 196,872. Those temporary measurement counters were absent from the timed binaries. The committed regression counts candidate-content bytes only in unit-test builds.

Ordinary prose/links and valid emphasis/code/math workloads scale approximately linearly over 10,000–40,000 paragraphs. A nine-run recheck after repository checks finished found CPU and wall-time differences below 1% and peak RSS differences below 0.1% at 40,000 paragraphs. Stdout/stderr hashes and exit status matched for every paired measured workload.

All 1,010 differential comparisons matched, covering existing CLI transcripts, second passes, mixed line endings, and batches of 4,096 short emphasis combinations. A focused transcript adds escapes, delimiter runs, late closers, Unicode whitespace, multiline boundaries, and literal/opaque contexts; existing expectations are unchanged. `scripts/check.sh` passed, including the existing allocation limits, 153 external tests, and 57 editor tests. Allocation limits supplement the CPU measurements; they do not establish bounded recognition work.

The deterministic regression formats Markdown through `format_source_report`, checks exact output, and bounds candidate-content scanning by four times the input length. It covers `*` and `_`, 32–128 openers, and valid late closers; a positive-count assertion verifies that the valid closer exercises the instrumentation. Applied to `095420c` with only the test and counter instrumentation, it fails at 32 openers: 31,744 bytes scanned for 122 input bytes, exceeding the 488-byte budget. It passes with the optimization. The follow-up passed `cargo fmt --check`, clippy with all targets/features, `cargo test --lib --test cli_cases --test literal_emphasis`, and 12 bounded before/after release output comparisons.

title: Preserve multiline code and math during Markdown formatting
description:
Preserve recognized inline code and math while formatting surrounding Markdown. Paragraph and container preparation currently treat whitespace inside multiline literals as ordinary line whitespace, which can delete literal bytes and leave surrounding prose, links, and emphasis unformatted.

## Changes

- Preserve spaces, tabs, escapes, and authored LF, CRLF, or CR line endings inside recognized literals, including mixed line endings. For example, the code contents represented by `first  \n  second [x]( url )` keep both spaces before the newline and both spaces after it.
- Format supported surrounding prose, real links, and emphasis in paragraphs, lists, blockquotes, definition lists, footnotes, and existing nested Markdown paths. Multiline literals remain indivisible wrapping tokens and may exceed the requested width.
- Remove container prefixes using authored structural indentation before normalizing content. This keeps literal whitespace separate from the indentation used when emitting the formatted container.

Internally, a flat set of source ranges retains literal boundaries and existing token identity using the current scanners and caches. Ordinary text and gaps remain implicit between ranges. Drafts retain source and recognition facts; resolution materializes only the form requested by the effective options. Canonicalization is skipped when disabled, and unwrapped output needs no measured token array. Later directives can derive another form from the retained source before emission.

Plans carry literal ranges through normalization and prefix restoration into the existing verbatim output mechanism, including nested Markdown output. Emission executes retained decisions. Editable whitespace and structural blank lines still receive normal cleanup. Document-level final-newline insertion remains active after terminal literals; explicit preservation and standalone shortcode tokens retain their existing EOF policy.

Exact-output CLI regressions cover wrapping modes, canonicalization, authored container indentation, list delimiter and opener boundaries, marker-only lines, document EOF boundaries, line endings, later directives, and second-pass idempotence. Compatibility controls retain ordinary gap cleanup, hard breaks outside literals, HTML, templates, and automatic fallback.

Existing container grammar, template eligibility, HTML/raw-angle policies, and malformed-delimiter boundaries remain in place. Recognition does not descend into opaque HTML or strikethrough. The existing label validator also leaves multiline literals inside link labels unsupported. Unsupported content keeps its existing fallback, whose trailing-space cleanup does not promise literal preservation or idempotence. See [the literal contract and boundaries](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/yamark/blob/36e4311/docs/inline-literals.md).

## Performance

**Faster on every measured workload with unchanged output.** Peak memory falls except for a small increase in unwrapped prose. Multiline containers use more memory and are slower when canonicalization is enabled; those workloads now preserve literal bytes and format surrounding content that main leaves unformatted.

- **Ordinary prose and links:** 11.2–17.1% faster. Peak memory is 14.3–14.5% lower with column wrapping; with wrapping disabled, it is 3.4–3.5% higher (about 0.6 MiB).
- **Dense single-line literals and multiline paragraphs:** 24.0–38.6% faster and 5.5–26.8% less peak memory. Output hashes match main for these and the prose/link workloads.
- **Multiline containers:** about 4.8% faster without canonicalization, but **3.8–8.0% slower** with it. Peak memory is **7.4–14.5% higher** (4.2–7.7 MiB).

The multiline-container workload has different output: main leaves 27,212 real links unformatted and removes trailing spaces inside those literals. With canonicalization enabled, it also leaves 27,212 surrounding emphasis spans unformatted. This change preserves those spaces and formats the surrounding content. These measurements therefore include that additional work; they are separate from the workloads with identical output.

title: Preserve explicitly skipped Markdown through output cleanup
description:
Explicitly skipped Markdown could still lose trailing whitespace when its output passed through Markdown cleanup, particularly when `fmt: skip file` selected a child fence or div. This PR makes those preserved bytes opaque to subsequent cleanup, using the output ranges introduced by #12.

Markdown nodes selected by `fmt: skip`, disabled regions selected by `fmt: off`, directive nodes with `EmitPlan::Preserve`, and whole Markdown documents/fragments selected by `fmt: skip file` retain their complete bytes. Protection survives the supported nested Markdown fence/div paths. Ordinary output between protected ranges still formats, and ordinary EOF cleanup still applies outside those ranges.

For example, with `--wrap sentence`, these lines inside a skipped child previously lost their two trailing spaces. Escaped strings make the byte difference visible:

```text
Input / new output: "message=\"keep   spacing\"  \n>}}\nKeep   this body.  \n"
Previous output:    "message=\"keep   spacing\"\n>}}\nKeep   this body.\n"
```

Outside the child, `"Format   outside the fence.\n"` still becomes `"Format outside the fence.\n"`. An explicitly skipped paragraph ending in `"Keep   é prose.  \t"` at EOF now retains the spaces, tab, and absent final newline.

Internally, `EmittedText` and `EmitOutput` carry syntax-independent `verbatim` output ranges, and `push_verbatim` replaces `push_shortcode`. Ranges are relative to the returned text, including when a child begins at a nonzero source offset. The recursive `push_preserved_node` child walk is removed: a preserved container contributes its complete source span. The skip-file early return marks the whole nonempty Markdown result without recovering token boundaries or adding content scans. Empty range vectors allocate no storage, and ordinary formatting gains no scanning or copying.

`EmitPlan::Copy`, unsupported formatting, and retained-plan preservation flags retain baseline cleanup. The parser and directive state are unchanged, including #12's linewise `fmt: on` boundary inside shortcode-, fence-, HTML-, or math-like disabled text. YAML, source-language adapters, reindentation, external formatters, inline recognition, wrapping, canonicalization, template policy, and configuration precedence are unchanged. Public CLI checks cover LF/CRLF/CR, mixed line endings, EOF without a newline, and second-pass idempotence. title: Keep inline literals intact when canonicalizing emphasis
description:
Prevent underscore and asterisk characters inside recognized inline code or math from closing surrounding emphasis. With `--canonical`, canonicalize the surrounding emphasis while copying literal contents unchanged.

For `format --stdin-file-path input.md --wrap none --canonical`:

```markdown

```

Main currently produces:

```markdown
# *Before `*a_ [x]( url )` after_
```

This PR produces:

```markdown
# *Before `_a_ [x]( url )` after*
```

The same fix applies through existing callers to ordinary paragraphs and supported list/blockquote content. Corrected emphasis boundaries also keep the whole emphasis span together during wrapping, including without `--canonical`. Some inputs previously failed inline tokenization and were copied unchanged; they now format surrounding prose and actual links. Literal link-like text stays exact.

Internally, `canonicalize_inline` and the emphasis closing search use the existing `InlineScan` code matcher and math scanner. Escaped candidates do not open literals. The existing failed-code-search cache also covers earlier positions revisited after unsuccessful emphasis lookahead and suffixes of unmatched runs already accepted by canonicalization. Preparation and canonical layouts remain lazy.

title: Preserve standalone shortcode tokens independently
description:
Standalone shortcode names previously determined whether Yamark formatted the text between them. This PR preserves each recognized `{{< ... >}}` or `{{% ... %}}` token independently while formatting is enabled, and lets intervening Markdown follow ordinary formatting rules. Opening, closing, and self-closing tokens have the same policy; names such as `raw`, `verbatim`, and `something.inline` have no special meaning.

Base: freshly fetched `origin/main` at `48440cf97405a6f753e2e5a71c9320e49feb4787`, the merge commit for #11. This remains the current main baseline. The independent-token work in #4 was read as a reference; neither #4 nor #6 was merged or cherry-picked, and both PRs are untouched.

With `--wrap sentence`, this input was previously preserved as a paired block:

```text
{{< notice >}}

First
sentence. Second
sentence.

{{< /notice >}}
```

It now formats as:

```text
{{< notice >}}

First sentence.
Second sentence.

{{< /notice >}}
```

While formatting is enabled, a forward-only lexical scanner finds each token's own delimiter outside single, double, and backtick quotes. It preserves token bytes, escapes, internal whitespace and line endings, a file-leading BOM, and a missing final newline. An unterminated token or quote preserves through the end of its enclosing Markdown document/fragment without searching outside that range or rescanning suffixes. Directive-looking text inside a recognized token is data; normal directive processing resumes after a complete token.

While formatting is disabled, the existing linewise directive policy applies. The disabled-region scan stops when `markdown_on_directive_line` recognizes `fmt: on`, even when that line appears inside text resembling a shortcode argument, fence, HTML, or math block. Authors can disable body formatting with `fmt: off/on`, subject to this linewise boundary. Disabled regions do not acquire shortcode or foreign-language structure.

Internally, this removes `HugoShortcodeOpening`, `hugo_shortcode_opening`, `find_hugo_shortcode_close`, and `hugo_shortcode_closes`. Recognition remains in parsing, retaining #7's prepared-plan/emission boundary. Recognized shortcode spans bypass destructive whitespace cleanup and retain their boundaries through supported nested Markdown fences/divs, including copying a container selected by `fmt: skip`. General Markdown cleanup is unchanged.

The correction removes the early disabled-mode `push_shortcode_token` path, the fence/comment tracking introduced for that path, and its `Fence::closes` helper. `markdown_disabled_region_end` and the enabled fence helpers now match the baseline exactly. This fixes the disabled HTML/math regression without adding raw-block categories. BOM handling, the enabled indented-code exclusion, token scanning, and targeted emission remain intact.

Placement, inline/container, and mixed-line support remain bounded by existing behavior. There are no changes to HTML recognition/matching, bare-template eligibility, `ParagraphTemplateSpans`, links, canonicalization, general inline parsing, public APIs, dependencies, configuration, or check infrastructure. This does not interpret template expressions or imply rendering equivalence for arbitrary Hugo/Jinja templates.

Known limitation: `fmt: skip file` already applies within recursively parsed Markdown fences/divs, scoped to that child document. Its early exit still allows the parent to trim trailing whitespace from the skipped fragment, including ordinary prose and shortcode arguments. `markdown_shortcode_nested_skip_file_known_bug.case` records the unchanged baseline bug; its expected output is not a preservation guarantee. The early exit remains, with no boundary recovery or emission-time rescanning.

The new `markdown_shortcode_disabled_html_math.case` fails at `83ecffe` and passes with the correction. It matches the baseline's stdout, stderr, and exit status. Existing disabled indented-code, fence, and comment cases are retained and also match the baseline. The `fmt: off` portion of `markdown_shortcode_directives.case` now resumes formatting at the first recognized `fmt: on`, restoring baseline output; its enabled-token checks are unchanged. Additional exact-byte checks cover directive-looking contents in enabled tokens, BOMs, LF/CRLF/CR, EOF without a newline, supported nested Markdown paths, and second-pass idempotence. `--verify` is not used as proof of Markdown literal preservation.

`cargo test --test cli_cases --test shortcodes` and the unchanged `scripts/check.sh` pass. The full gate includes fmt, strict Clippy, all Rust tests, 153 external Python tests, and 57 VS Code tests.

Release comparisons use Rust 1.98.1 on aarch64-apple-darwin and `cargo build --release --locked` for both revisions. Among the 106 baseline transcripts, exactly two outputs intentionally change: `markdown_div_shortcode_math.case` formats the formerly preserved body, and `markdown_shortcode_quoted_closing_delimiter.case` preserves the complete quoted token before formatting the following paragraph. The corresponding paired-body assertion in `spec_cli.rs` is also updated. All other baseline stdout, stderr, and exit statuses are identical. Compared with `83ecffe`, only the disabled directive expectation changes among its 117 existing transcripts; the other 116 remain identical.

Performance measurements were collected at `5887134`, using fresh baseline and branch release builds with the same toolchain and flags, without `RUSTFLAGS`. Temporary CLI probes used one warmup and alternating baseline/branch runs: 11 repetitions for ordinary workloads, five for token scaling, and seven for bodies and disabled regions. CPU is child user+system time from `wait4`; memory is peak RSS. No benchmark infrastructure or timing-sensitive CI tests were added.

The existing `tools/bench/big.R` generator (default seed) supplied three approximately 4 MB ordinary workloads, formatted with `--wrap 80`. Their stdout, stderr, and status are identical:

| Workload                  | Baseline CPU | Branch CPU | Baseline / branch RSS |
| ------------------------- | -----------: | ---------: | --------------------: |
| `big.md`                  |     85.33 ms |   85.34 ms |     26.08 / 26.03 MiB |
| `big.yaml`                |     63.68 ms |   62.33 ms |     51.88 / 51.89 MiB |
| `big-with-frontmatter.md` |     82.58 ms |   82.76 ms |     27.27 / 27.14 MiB |

No material ordinary-workload CPU or memory regression was observed. Median CPU differences range from -2.1% to +0.2%; the largest peak RSS increase is 0.02 MiB.

For `--wrap sentence`, alternating `{{< call value="one" >}}` and `{{% call /%}}` lines have no named closing tags. Outputs are identical, while the removed suffix searches no longer dominate:

| Independent calls | Baseline CPU | Branch CPU |
| ----------------: | -----------: | ---------: |
|             1,000 |      5.07 ms |    2.74 ms |
|             2,000 |     11.47 ms |    2.98 ms |
|             4,000 |     32.09 ms |    3.29 ms |
|             8,000 |    120.98 ms |    4.42 ms |
|            16,000 |    457.75 ms |    6.77 ms |

A single unterminated quoted token containing repeated `Keep   quoted >}} data.  ` lines takes 3.79 ms at 1.09 MB, 5.31 ms at 2.18 MB, 8.35 ms at 4.36 MB, 13.74 ms at 8.72 MB. The branch output is checked against the exact input. At the largest size, baseline/branch CPU is 293.84/13.74 ms and RSS is 215.23/28.03 MiB. Baseline output differs because it formats token contents. The scanner makes one forward pass through the bounded remainder.

Separately, 10,000 paired blocks with two short sentences (0.69 MB) take 5.86 → 23.11 ms CPU and 10.06 → 23.67 MiB RSS. This workload intentionally changes output: the branch now plans and formats the previously copied bodies. It is distinct from overhead on unchanged output.

The disabled-region probe repeats `fmt: off`, a fence-looking line, and `fmt: on`. At 1,000/2,000/4,000/8,000/16,000 regions, branch CPU is 3.55, 4.67, 6.11, 9.74, 15.91 ms.
